claims.text: The initial single-phase fcc Fe-Co-Ni-Ti alloy has coercivity below 10 Oe.
The low coercivity of the single-phase alloy results from suppressed orbital moments and weak magnetic anisotropy.
Adding Ti beyond its solid-solubility limit and applying heat treatment will precipitate a Ti-rich secondary phase in the fcc matrix.
The precipitated Ti-rich phase may be a C14 Laves phase or another Ti-based intermetallic.
The fcc matrix and Ti-rich secondary phase will remain stable without secondary-phase dissolution over 300-600 K.
The Ti-rich precipitates will be nanoscale to microscale and distributed throughout the fcc matrix.
The Ti-rich precipitates will form coherent or semi-coherent interfaces with the fcc matrix.
The precipitate interfaces will act as magnetic-domain-wall pinning centers.
The Ti-rich phase will alter the local magnetic ground state through interfacial exchange coupling.
The Ti-rich phase will introduce local strain fields and modify electronic structure at fcc/precipitate interfaces.
Interfacial electronic-structure modification will enhance orbital-moment contributions and magnetic anisotropy in adjacent fcc regions.
A non-magnetic or weakly magnetic Ti-rich barrier will suppress orbital-moment quenching in adjacent fcc matrix regions.
Domain-wall pinning at fcc/precipitate interfaces will increase the field required for wall motion and thereby increase coercivity.
The dual-phase alloy will exhibit coercivity exceeding 100 Oe.
The dual-phase alloy will have moderately lower saturation magnetization than the single-phase alloy.
The dual-phase alloy will retain a magnetic ordering temperature above room temperature.
The proposed mechanism is expected to operate for Ti concentrations between 5 and 15 at.%.
Excessive Ti can produce brittle phases or transform the material completely to non-fcc structures.
The effectiveness of domain-wall pinning depends on precipitate size, distribution, and interfacial coherence.

A controlled comparison of phase-confirmed single-phase and dual-phase alloys, using coercivity and saturation-magnetization measurements up to 600 K, can test the hypothesis; confirmed dual-phase material remaining below 100 Oe, single-phase material exceeding 100 Oe, or ordering below room temperature are specified adverse outcomes.
